Elastic Constants: E, ν, λ, μ

Conversion table for isotropic elastic constants

In the lecture notes, (1.13) and (1.14) give the relationship between the pair \((E,\nu)\) and \((\mu, \lambda)\). You can find a full relationship table between each parameters on Wikipedia.

Poisson’s ratio — what does it mean?

Pull a bar and it usually gets thinner — that lateral response is set by \(\nu\). Try the presets below: cork (\(\nu\approx0\)), typical metals (\(\nu\approx0.3\)), rubber (\(\nu\approx0.499\), nearly incompressible), and auxetic foam (\(\nu<0\), gets fatter when stretched).

Pull a bar along its length — ν sets how much it shrinks (or grows) sideways
Lateral strain ε_lat = −νε
Length change
Width change
Volume change ΔV/V₀
Pull most ordinary materials and they get thinner as they get longer — that's a positive Poisson's ratio. ν=0 means no lateral response at all (like cork, which is why it's easy to push into a bottle without swelling out the sides). ν=0.5 means the material can't change volume — it must get thinner by exactly the amount needed to conserve volume (rubber, most fluids). Negative ν ("auxetic") materials do the opposite of intuition: pull them and they get fatter, not thinner.

Lamé constants ↔︎ (E, ν)

\[ \mu = \frac{E}{2(1+\nu)}, \qquad \lambda = \frac{E\nu}{(1+\nu)(1-2\nu)}, \qquad K = \frac{E}{3(1-2\nu)} \]

Live isotropic elasticity conversion and 6×6 Voigt stiffness matrix (order 11,22,33,23,13,12)
Approaching the incompressible limit (ν → 0.5): λ and K diverge. Common for rubber-like materials; not physical for most metals/alloys.

DERIVED CONSTANTS

λ (Lamé's first parameter)
μ = G (shear modulus)
K (bulk modulus)
μ = E / [2(1+ν)]  ·  λ = Eν / [(1+ν)(1−2ν)]  ·  K = E / [3(1−2ν)] = λ + 2μ/3

λ(ν) AT FIXED E — SINGULARITY AT ν=0.5

ISOTROPIC STIFFNESS MATRIX C (VOIGT)

C relates Voigt stress and (engineering-shear) strain vectors: σ_V = C·ε_V, with the diagonal shear terms equal to μ (not 2μ) because γ_ij = 2ε_ij already carries the factor of two. Off-diagonal 4-5-6 blocks are zero for an isotropic material — normal and shear response never couple.

What do λ and μ mean physically?

\(\mu\) resists pure shape change (shear). \(\lambda\) is subtler — it’s the stress that appears sideways only when lateral strain is prevented (confined loading), not something you’d feel in a free pull test.

μ resists shape change; λ is the stress that shows up sideways when shape change is prevented

μ — resistance to shape change

γ = τ/μ =

λ — sideways stress when confined

Set the axial stress σ on a bar between rigid walls (ε_lateral locked at 0); ε_axial = σ/(λ+2μ)
ε_axial = σ/(λ+2μ) =
σ_wall = λε =
Left: apply a shear stress τ and read off the resulting angle γ = τ/μ — no volume or lateral coupling involved, just μ resisting the change of shape. Right: apply an axial stress σ to a bar whose sides are clamped so it can't bulge or neck sideways (ε_lateral = 0 by construction, not by Poisson relaxation) — the walls still feel a push or pull, and that reaction is exactly λε. λ isn't a "stiffness" you can feel directly in an unconstrained pull test (that's E); it only shows up once something stops the material from doing what its Poisson's ratio would otherwise let it do. Note λ+2μ = M, the constrained (uniaxial-strain) modulus — the same quantity that sets P-wave speed in geomechanics/seismology. If λ+2μ ≤ 0 (possible at the low end of these sliders) the material is unstable and the strain readout is suppressed rather than shown as a nonsense sign.
